Convert time from string representation to a pandas timestamp. To utc timestamps becuase its currently Madrid timezone timestamp which uses daylights savings causing there when swapping from +1 to +2 you skip an hour making it not a consistant time index like utc.

Distrubtion of forecast_solar_day_ahead is heavly skewed towards the right with 8000 observations concentraded around 0.This suggest that low solar energy forecasts are common, potentially due to periods of when little or no solar energy is being generated such as at night.The right long tail indicates that that higher solar energy forecasts occur less frequently.The mean(1439.07 MW) being considerably higher than median further supports the strong right skew.The boxplot supports the right-skewed distrubtion as the median is near the bottom and the upper whisker is longer than lower whisker.No statistically outliers where identified by the boxplot.

Distrubtion of forecast_wind_onshore_day_ahead is swewed towards the right but not as severly as forecast_solar_day_ahead.The minimum forecast is 237 MW suggesting that the forecast_wind_onshore predicts that there will be some energy generated.That these values are more spreadout than forecast_solar_day_ahead with highest frequency reaching approximately 900 observations.The predictions are concentrated around wind_onshore_day_ahead generating between 2000 and 7000 MW.With higher values appearing less frequently.The large standard deviation suggests that there is susbstantial variation in forecast wind generation.The mean is 5,471.22 MW, which is higher than the median of 4,855 MW, further supporting the right skew.The box plot shows several high value outliers above the top whisker approximately starting at 13500 MW and ending approxiametly at 17500.

Distrubtion of total_load_forecast has a roughly bimodal distrubtion with 2 main peaks around 24000 MW and 31000 MW.The distrubtiion is realtivly symmestrical, with no signigicant skew towards either side. This suggests that there are 2 common levels of forecast electricity demand.The quartiles being so close with 25%(28712.13) 50% (28906.00) and 75%(32263.25) show us that while it has bimodal distrubtion the overall distubtion is quite relative symetric and has no long tails as we can see from the min (28712.13) and max values (41390.00) shows the range of the forecast electricty demand.The boxplot further supports the relatively symmetrical distribution with the median positioned near the centre of the box and reasonably balanced whiskers and no statistical outliers are identified.

Distrubtion of price_day_ahead there is a roughly normal distrubtion of price_day_ahead and with a slighly skew towards the left.Most observations are concentrated around €40/MWh and €65/MWh with the peak being around €50/MWh.The slight left skew can be seen as the tail extending towards lower prices.There are obviously no prices of €0/MWh with the minium being €2.06 but there is a higher number of observations around the left tail compared to the right tail of expensive prices.This suggest that unsually low day ahead prices occured more frequently than unsually high prices.The boxplot shows outliers at both ends of distrubtion.With the low price outliers starting at €12 going down to €2.06 and the high price outliers starting at €90 and going up to €101.99.

Distrubtion of price_actual has a roughly normal distubtion with a more left skew than price_day_ahead.Most observations are conventrated around €45/MWh to 65/MWh.The pattern with tails for high and low prices remains the same.This suggest that the pattern of low prices occuring more frequently that the expensive prices remains true for price_actual.The pattern continous for boxplots there are outliers at both ends of distrubtion.With the low price outliers starting at €22 going down to €9.33 and the high price outliers starting at €95 and going up to €116.80.The mean is of price actual is € 57.88 vs day ahead price of €49.87.The metrics suggests that in the period measured the price actual is more expensive than day ahead price.

Preproccesing

Madrid time is used as for creating local calender features such as hour ,day of week,day of the year,month and the cyclical encoding of the hours

In [126]:
def create_time_features(dataset):
    dataset=dataset.copy()
    
    local_time=convert_utc_index_to_madrid(dataset)
    dataset["hour"]=local_time.hour
    dataset["day_of_week"]=local_time.day_of_week
    dataset["day_of_year"]=local_time.day_of_year
    dataset["month"]=local_time.month
    dataset["hour_sin"]=np.sin(2*np.pi*dataset["hour"]/24)
    dataset["hour_cos"]=np.cos(2*np.pi*dataset["hour"]/24)

    return dataset

For my final test set I am using the 2018 this uses up 25% of my entire dataset I believe it is worth having the less training data to ensure that that the prediction get a fair one year of predictons. The price actual is my target set becuase it is the price of the that is if you bought the electricy at the time stamp. The features are the price day ahead which is paid 24 hours in advance for electricy generated at the hour of the timestamp and forecasts of generation or demand for the timestamp.

target_col_in_energy_dataset=filtered_energy_dataset["price_actual"].copy()

print(f"filtered\n{filtered_energy_dataset.iloc[1].to_string()}\nindex of filtered\n{filtered_energy_dataset.index}\n"

      f"\n\ntarget_col_in_energy_dataset\n{target_col_in_energy_dataset.iloc[1]}\n index of target\n{target_col_in_energy_dataset.index}\n")

I am using timeseriessplit for cross validation becuase my data is time ordered and temporal. N_splits is 24 becuase that how many month is in 2 years test_size is 24*30 =720 is to represent 30 calendery days instead of an exact month.

cv_results_linear_regression = cross_validate(
    linear_regression_pipeline,
    features_train,
    target_train,
    cv=time_series_cv_splitter,
    scoring={
        "mae": "neg_mean_absolute_error",
        "rmse": "neg_root_mean_squared_error",
        "r2": "r2"
    },
    
)

# Convert negative error scores back to positive errors becuase cross validation follows the rule that higher scores are better but for MAE and RSME lower errors are better  
fold_results = pd.DataFrame({
    "MAE": -cv_results_linear_regression["test_mae"],
    "RMSE": -cv_results_linear_regression["test_rmse"],
    "R2": cv_results_linear_regression["test_r2"]
})
fold_results.index.name = "Fold"


display("Results for each fold",fold_results)
display("Fold aggregate results",fold_results.agg(["mean", "std","min","max"]))

pipeline_hgb_to_tune = clone(hist_gradient_boosting_pipeline)

pipeline_hgb_to_tune.set_params(histgradientboostingregressor__early_stopping=False)

search_hgb_learn_itr=GridSearchCV(estimator=pipeline_hgb_to_tune,
                                  param_grid={
                                  
                                    "histgradientboostingregressor__learning_rate": [0.03, 0.035,0.04],
                                    "histgradientboostingregressor__max_iter": [150, 250, 300],  
                                  },
                                  cv=time_series_cv_splitter,
                                  scoring={
                                      "mae": "neg_mean_absolute_error",
                                      "rmse": "neg_root_mean_squared_error",
                                       "r2": "r2",  
                                  },
                                  refit="rmse",
                                  n_jobs=-1,
                                  verbose=2,
                                      )
search_hgb_learn_itr.fit(features_train, target_train)

print("Best Parameters:",search_hgb_learn_itr.best_params_)
print(f"RMSE:€ {-search_hgb_learn_itr.best_score_:.3f} MWh")

best_hgb_pipeline_found_in_search = search_hgb_learn_itr.best_estimator_

Fitting 24 folds for each of 9 candidates, totalling 216 fits
Best Parameters: {'histgradientboostingregressor__learning_rate': 0.035, 'histgradientboostingregressor__max_iter': 250}
RMSE:€ 9.075 MWh

Grid-search tuning results¶

I used GridSearchCV with RMSE as the selection metric. Each search narrowed the parameter ranges around the strongest result from the previous search.

Search max_iter values tested learning_rate values tested Best max_iter Best learning_rate Best RMSE
1 300, 1000, 2000 0.03, 0.05, 0.10 300 0.030 €9.076/MWh
2 250, 300, 350 0.025, 0.03, 0.035 250 0.035 €9.075/MWh
3 150, 250, 300 0.030, 0.035, 0.040 250 0.035 €9.075/MWh

The second and third searches produced the same best configuration a learning rate of 0.035 and 250 iterations. Compared with the first search, this reduced RMSE from €9.076/MWh to €9.075/MWh, so further narrowing produced no meaningful improvement.

def rf_random_search (search_paramaters):
    rf_random_search=RandomizedSearchCV(estimator=pipeline_rf_to_tune,
                                    param_distributions=search_paramaters,
                                    n_iter=30,
                                    random_state=42,
                                    cv=time_series_cv_splitter,
                                    scoring={
                                        "mae": "neg_mean_absolute_error",
                                        "rmse": "neg_root_mean_squared_error",
                                        "r2": "r2",  
                                    },
                                    refit="rmse",
                                    n_jobs=-1,
                                    verbose=3,
                                        )
    rf_random_search.fit(features_train, target_train)

    results_rf_random_search = pd.DataFrame(rf_random_search.cv_results_)
    rf_random_search_results_table = pd.DataFrame({
        "CV RMSE":
                -results_rf_random_search["mean_test_rmse"],
        "n_estimators":
            results_rf_random_search["param_randomforestregressor__n_estimators"],

        "max_depth":
            results_rf_random_search["param_randomforestregressor__max_depth"],

        "min_samples_leaf":
            results_rf_random_search["param_randomforestregressor__min_samples_leaf"],

        "max_features":
            results_rf_random_search["param_randomforestregressor__max_features"],
    })

    rf_random_search_results_table = rf_random_search_results_table.sort_values(
        "CV RMSE",
        ascending=True
    ).reset_index(drop=True)

    display(rf_random_search_results_table)


    print("Best Parameters:",rf_random_search.best_params_)
    print(f"RMSE:€ {-rf_random_search.best_score_:.3f} MWh")
   

    return rf_random_search.best_estimator_

def grid_search_rf(search_params):
    search_rf_params=GridSearchCV(estimator=pipeline_rf_to_tune,
                                  param_grid=search_params,
                                  cv=time_series_cv_splitter,
                                  scoring={
                                      "mae": "neg_mean_absolute_error",
                                      "rmse": "neg_root_mean_squared_error",
                                       "r2": "r2",  
                                  },
                                  refit="rmse",
                                   
                                  n_jobs=-1,
                                  verbose=2,
                                      )
    search_rf_params.fit(features_train, target_train)

    print("Best Parameters:",search_rf_params.best_params_)
    print(f"RMSE:€ {-search_rf_params.best_score_:.3f} MWh")
    display_random_forest_fine_tuning_results(search_rf_params,5);
    return search_rf_params

Started with RandomizedSearchCV for 30 iterations instead of GridSearch as GridSearch would take to long with this many  parameters to tune.This is becuase the more parameters to tune increases the search area and to keep the compute and time to try different parameters reasonable RandomizedSearchCV was the practical choice for the coarse searches. The configurations were ranked by mean RMSE across the same 24 time-series cross-validation folds.


The first Search considered 50,100 and 200 tree’s. Its best configuration used 100 trees, a maximum dept of None, a minimum leaf size of 5 and a max features of 0.5 this configuration got a RMSE score of 9.045762.


The second search tested 100,300 and 500 trees to investigate whether larger forests improved performance. The best configuration in this search used 100 trees, a maximum depth of 10 and a minimum leaf size of 5 and max features of 0.5. This configuration got a RMSE score of 9.041078 which is an improvement of only 0.004684 €/MWh, suggesting little practical gain..


I choose to use 100 trees after the first grid search becuase computation time grows with number of trees and the top 3 results had 100 trees therefore there was little reason to pay for a larger forest of 500.Fixing the number of trees at 100 allowed me to try more combinations of the remaining parameters and swap to gridsearch.For following searches I based it on the top 5 results from previous searches.Then I choose next parameters to be the best performing parameters as well as values around these top performing values or those in a trending direction e.g if highest value parameter was performing the best add more higher values and remove the lower values.I stopped after three grid searches because the final two selected the same best parameters: 100 trees, a maximum depth of 12, a minimum leaf size of 7 and max_features of 0.4. This achieved a mean CV RMSE of 9.037118 €/MWh. The small improvement over the coarse searches suggested limited benefit from further tuning within these parameter ranges.

In [ ]:






plot_residuals(target_test,hgb_test_prediction,"Histogram Gradient Boosting")
plot_residuals_over_time(target_test,hgb_test_prediction,"Histogram Gradient Boosting")
plot_residuals(target_test,rf_test_prediction,"Random Forest")
plot_residuals_over_time(target_test,rf_test_prediction,"Random Forest")

















































































The residual diagnostics for the random forest and histogram gradient boosting models are very similar.They are biased at the extremes of the predicted range.Past 80 €/MWh the residuals are almost all negative so the models overpredict the highest prices and below 40 €/MWh predictions are few and widely scattered. Elsewhere, most errors fall within a range of +10 €/MWh and -10 €/MWh.Most Predicted prices fall within 45 to 75.


When we look at residuals overtime a pattern becomes clear for both models.They both make specific errors during specific periods.In early January the model overpredicts the price.Down to around -59 €/MWh for histogram gradient boosting and for random forest  down to around -49  €/MWh.The other period is from September to October where prices are underpredicted of 10 €/MWh to €25 €/MWh.These errors persits for weeks at a time suggesting that the models miss the changes that  influces the prices.This suggest that failure is due to either the feature and or the limitations of tree based approaches  but the residual plots alone cannot establish the cause.

results_table = pd.DataFrame([
    {
        "Model": name,
        "Test MAE (€/MWh)": mean_absolute_error(target_test, predictions),
        "Test RMSE (€/MWh)": root_mean_squared_error(target_test, predictions),
        "Test R²": r2_score(target_test, predictions),
    }
    for name, predictions in model_predictions.items()
]).set_index("Model")

    100 * (baseline_rmse - results_table["Test RMSE (€/MWh)"])/ baseline_rmse
)

Linear regression the baseline was the strongest model on the held out 2018 test period.It achieved the MAE (5.525 €/MWh), lowest RMSE (8.429 €/MWh), and highest R² (0.524).The tuned Random Forest and Histogram Gradient Boosting models did not improve on the baseline suggesting that their additional complexity did not provide better predicitions in this experiment.These findings are limited to the selected features and one test year.They do not establish that linear regression is always superior.


Next Steps


I will compare errors across temporal validation periods and test whether additional predictors available at forecast time reduce sustained overprediction and underprediction.


The residual analysis showed sustained overprediction in January and underprediction during September and October for both tree-based models. Next, I will investigate possible causes by comparing demand forecasts, renewable generation forecasts and the difference between day-ahead and actual prices during these periods with periods of better performance. This may help identify whether the errors are associated with unusual conditions or changes in relationships learned from the training data, and guide further feature or model improvements.


One potential improvement is to treat day of the week and month as categorical features in Histogram Gradient Boosting. This would allow the model to group days or months according to their relationship with electricity prices and may help capture calendar patterns. I will tune the hyperparameters using the same training data and time-series cross-validation splits as the existing model to assess whether this improves performance.
